title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hookLine: before dawn in the South, Krishna breaks Naraka's fortress open and the captives walk free
carry: god comes down to set the captive free
last: EKAM SAT: ONE TRUTH, MANY NAMES.

lines: WARM OIL, A HOT BATH, NEW CLOTHES.
cards: In Tamil Nadu, a family's Deepavali can begin around four in the morning. Someone wakes the house while it's still pitch dark. Each person sits down, and an elder rubs warm sesame oil into their hair.
Then a hot bath, new clothes, a firecracker before sunrise, sweets for breakfast. In North India, Diwali is usually a night: the lamps come out after dark, for Rama coming home. Same festival name.
Different hour, different story. This one isn't about Rama at all.

teach.h: NARAKA: A CRUEL KING, A FORTRESS.
teach.b: The story belongs to Krishna and a demon king named Naraka, and the Bhagavata Purana tells it. Naraka has grown arrogant and cruel.
He has stolen treasures from the gods, among them the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and he holds thousands of young women captive in his fortress city.
Krishna flies there on Garuda, his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks through the fortress walls, and kills Naraka in battle. Then he opens the fortress.
The women held there, sixteen thousand one hundred in the Bhagavata's count, walk out free. In the text they choose him as their husband, and he sends them to Dvaraka and marries them all.

Many families add that Naraka, dying, asked for his day to be remembered with lights. That's Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before the main Diwali night, and in much of South India it is Deepavali, kept before dawn.
The oil bath, people say, recalls Krishna bathing after the battle. Now the teaching under it.

teach.h: AVATAR: THE ONE WHO COMES DOWN.
teach.b: For Hindus, Krishna is Vishnu come down into the world: an avatar, a word that means one who descends.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says why he comes: whenever goodness is failing, age after age, he takes birth to protect the good and set things right. So the lamps aren't only for a win.
They're for a God who doesn't stay far off while people are trapped.

teach.h: GOD COMES DOWN TO SET THE CAPTIVE FREE.
teach.b: He comes down, breaks the walls, and opens the door. Rama coming home, the captives walking free: two roads to the same row of lamps.

how: In much of South India, Deepavali is celebrated before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi with an oil bath, new clothes, firecrackers and sweets; in many other regions that day is a smaller lamp-lighting the day before the main Diwali night.

s: every region keeps Diwali on the same night for the same reason
in much of the South it's kept before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi, for Krishna's victory.
after the battle, Krishna frees the women held captive in the fortress
the Bhagavata gives their number as sixteen thousand one hundred.
for Hindus, Krishna is Vishnu come down into the world to protect the good.

games.q: a friend asks why Hindus say Krishna "came down." by today's teaching, what fits?
o: Vishnu takes birth, age after age, whenever goodness is failing, to protect the good.
Krishna was a wise man who climbed up to heaven by his own effort.
God sends helpers to earth but never comes himself.
games.why: that's the avatar: in the Gita, Krishna says he comes whenever goodness fails. Naraka's fortress was one of those times.

practice: Many families set a small clay lamp, a diya, at the front door on Deepavali. Light one small light, or picture one. Think of someone who is stuck somewhere: a hard job, an illness, a lonely stretch.
If you pray, say a name of Krishna or Vishnu and ask for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind beside the light, at the door of the place they're stuck. You don't have to fix anything.
Just keep the lamp at their door.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. In much of the South, Deepavali comes before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi, remembering Krishna's victory and the captives set free.

orig.note: Sanskrit naraka (the king's name) + caturdaśī (the fourteenth lunar day): the day before the main Diwali night.

carryVoice: Your line: god comes down to set the captive free. That's what the lamp at the door remembers. See you tomorrow.
